posts.title: The agentic web is arriving through the back office
posts.excerpt: Agents won't browse your website the way people do. They'll book, enrol and pay through whatever your site exposes as a clear, callable step. Most small organisations aren't ready, and the fix is smaller than it sounds.
posts.text: There's a version of the "agentic web" story that's all about the front end: an assistant that reads web pages, clicks buttons and fills in forms on your behalf. It makes good demos. In practice, the first agents that get real work done won't win by being better at clicking. They'll win because the organisation on the other side has said, in a form a machine can rely on, what can be done and how. Most of that work happens in the back office. What an agent needs from a website Take a sports club, with a public website and a membership process behind it. A parent wants to register a child for the winter season. Today that means reading three pages, downloading a form, paying through a separate link and waiting for someone to reply to an email. An agent acting for that parent needs four things the website rarely provides: - What can be done. "Register a junior player for winter season" as a named action, not a paragraph of prose. - What it needs. Date of birth, an emergency contact, the age group. Typed fields, not "please include". - What it costs, and the rules. Fees, deadlines, the cases that need a committee decision. - What happens next. A confirmation it can hand back: registered, waitlisted, or "a person will review this". None of that is a design problem. It's a process problem that happens to surface on the website. The process is the product Clubs and small organisations that automate well do the same thing first: they write the process down as steps, each with one owner. The membership workflow becomes receive the registration → check eligibility → take payment → add to the roster → confirm. Some steps are software. Some are a volunteer with a spreadsheet. One or two are a committee decision that should never be automated. Once that's written down, three things become cheap: 1. Automating the dull steps. Payment, roster updates and confirmation emails run on their own. 2. Showing people what's going on. Every registration has a status someone can look up. 3. Opening the door to agents. The same steps, described with their inputs and outcomes, are exactly what an agent needs to act on someone's behalf. The agentic web isn't a new website. It's your existing process, written down clearly enough that software on either side can rely on it. Where to start Don't start with an "AI strategy". Start with the one process people complain about most, usually bookings, enrolments or memberships, and do three things: - Write the steps down, with an owner for each, and mark the ones that need judgement. - Automate one step end to end, including what happens when it fails. - Publish the result as a clear action: a form whose fields match the steps, and a confirmation that says exactly what happened. That's useful for people today. It's also, quietly, what makes your organisation reachable when the agents arrive. In the next issues, I'll walk through real (anonymised) examples: the sports club's membership workflow, a venue's booking flow, and what changed when each step got one owner.

posts.title: Testing integrations against digital twins
posts.excerpt: You can't run a test suite against a live mailing list. A small, faithful stand-in for each vendor API lets the real workflow files run end to end on every change, without sending anything to anyone.
posts.text: Integrations are where automations usually break, and they are also the hardest part to test. A test that sends a real campaign to a real list isn't a test. A test that mocks everything proves only that the mocks agree with each other. The middle ground used here is a digital twin of each vendor API. What a twin is A twin is a small in-memory stand-in for one provider, written from that provider's own API reference. It answers only the operations the workflow actually uses, with the same paths, fields and error codes. Anything else gets a clear "not in the twin" error, so a workflow can't quietly depend on behaviour nobody captured. It also keeps the provider's important rules. The newsletter's twin, for example, models double opt-in: a new contact stays pending until they confirm, and a campaign reaches only confirmed contacts. A campaign can be sent once; a second send is refused, as the real service refuses it. Running the real files The point is to run the actual workflow definitions, not a re-implementation of them. The tests load the same flow files that get deployed, run them step by step, and route every vendor call to the twin through the same HTTP interface the live system uses. So a scenario such as "a reader subscribes, confirms, and receives exactly one email for a new post, even when the post is published twice" exercises the code that will really run. Checking the tests themselves A green test suite only means something if it can go red. One cheap habit: break the logic on purpose — for example, make the "has this post been sent?" check always say no — and confirm the tests fail. If they still pass, they weren't testing what you thought. Where twins stop A twin is only as good as its reading of the provider's documentation. So before anything goes live, the same workflow runs once against the real service with a test list, and any difference found there is fixed in the twin first, then in the workflow. After that, the twin keeps every later change honest at no cost and with no risk.

posts.title: Running a coding agent unattended: what has to be true first
posts.excerpt: Letting an AI coding agent work on a server while nobody watches is less about the agent and more about the rails: typed specifications, scripts instead of clicks, hard stop rules and evidence in place of summaries.
posts.text: Part of the work behind this blog is done by an AI coding agent, Claude Code, running on a small server and taking the next piece of work from a queue. Making that safe had little to do with prompting. It came down to a handful of rules that would make sense for any new team member working alone at night. Judgement ends in a file Every piece of work starts from a written specification in the repository: the outcome, the acceptance checks, the constraints, and the decisions already made. The agent doesn't decide what to build. It decides how, within that file. When something genuinely needs a person, such as a missing credential, a choice between two designs or anything that publishes to the world, it stops and asks instead of guessing. Scripts, not clicks Deployments, workflow changes and checks run through scripts kept in the repository. The same command produces the same result every time, and its output is the record. Interactive connectors are allowed only as a named fallback when no script exists yet, and each use is followed by writing the script. Hard boundaries Some limits are enforced outside the agent, not just written in its instructions: - Credentials are scoped. A key for a test site can't be used to reach a live one. - Live client systems are out of bounds unless a person has released that exact action. - Commands that could destroy or publish something need an explicit go-ahead. When a boundary blocks the agent, the right outcome is a clear note of what it needed and why, not a workaround. Evidence over narrative "Done" means the acceptance checks ran and passed, with their output kept. Reports separate what changed in the code from what changed on running systems, and mark anything not actually observed as unknown. Retries are bounded: an unchanged failure isn't run again in the hope it passes. What it's good for With those rails, an agent is very good at careful, well-specified work: extending an integration, writing the tests that prove it, and leaving a precise list of what still needs a human. Without them, it's a fast way to make confident mistakes.

posts.title: One home per function
posts.excerpt: Most operational mess comes from the same fact living in two places. A simple rule — each function has one home, and everything else links to it — removes a surprising amount of coordination work.
posts.text: Small teams rarely fail for lack of tools. They fail because the same thing is tracked in three of them. The task is in the tracker, its status is in a chat thread, and the real decision is in someone's email. Every update then has to be made three times, and one of them is always stale. The rule used here is blunt: every function has one home. Everything else links to it. What "a function" means A function is a kind of work with its own owner and lifecycle. A few examples: - Planning the platform lives in one tracker, with its statuses. - Delivering work for a client lives in a separate system, with its statuses, owned by whoever manages delivery. - Decisions live in a decisions log in the repository, each with who made it and when. - Code and specifications live in the repository, and nowhere else is the source. The two trackers never mirror each other. If platform work needs to know that a delivery happened, it records a link to the delivery's receipt, not a copy of its status. One fact, one place The same idea applies inside a repository. A business's configuration is written once, in that business's own folder. Its parent folder doesn't repeat it; location says where it belongs. Generated files, such as an index agents read to find their way around, are produced from those sources and never edited by hand. Why it matters more with agents People can reconcile two slightly different notes in their heads. Software can't, and neither can an AI assistant reading the repository. When an agent finds two answers, it either picks one or stops. With one home per function there is only one answer to find, and the agent can be told exactly where to look. How to start Pick the function that causes the most "which one is right?" questions. Choose its single home, move the authoritative copy there, and replace every other copy with a link. Then make the rule explicit: if it isn't in the home, it isn't true yet.

posts.title: Making this blog an open agentic website
posts.excerpt: This site now carries an assistant that answers from its own posts and can subscribe a reader, running entirely in the visitor's browser on their own AI key. Here's what that took on a static site, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
posts.text: The first issue argued that the agentic web arrives through clearly described actions. This blog now tries that on itself. Its home page has an assistant that answers questions from the posts here and can subscribe a reader to the newsletter. It follows an open specification for "agentic websites", so other agent sites can find and call it too. Nothing runs on our server The site is still static. The assistant's runtime loads in the visitor's browser, and the visitor brings their own key for an AI provider, entered in the assistant's settings. The site pays nothing per question and holds nobody's key. The trade-off is stated plainly on the page: the visitor's messages, and the posts the assistant reads, go to the provider they choose. What the assistant can call The assistant can only use actions the site registers, each with typed inputs: - List posts, read a post and search posts, all reading from an index the site builds from the same posts you're reading. - Subscribe, which uses the same Brevo form as the subscribe box on the page. The first three only read. Subscribing contacts someone, so it is marked as an action that can't be undone: the browser shows the reader a confirmation dialog with their email address before anything is sent, and Brevo still sends its own confirmation email afterwards. Grounding, by design The assistant's instructions say facts come only from the site's own tools. It shouldn't invent posts, and when nothing here covers a question it should say the blog hasn't written about it yet. It also has a short list of what the site can't do, such as taking on client work, so it declines those plainly instead of improvising. Published for other agents The site publishes a manifest and a description of its agent network at public addresses. Another agent website can run this network for its own visitor, on that visitor's key. When it does, it gets none of this site's actions: it can say what the blog covers and point to the page, but it can't subscribe anyone. That boundary is deliberate. What's still rough The specification asks for every change to be shown to the visitor before it runs. The runtime used here only does that for actions marked irreversible, which is one reason subscribing is marked that way. Expect this page to change as the tools mature.

posts.title: What MCP is, and why it matters to small teams
posts.excerpt: The Model Context Protocol gives AI assistants one standard way to reach tools and data. It lowers the cost of connecting things, but a connector you click through every time is still not automation.
posts.text: The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open standard for connecting AI applications to the tools and data they need. A service publishes an MCP server that lists what it can do, each tool with a name, a description and typed inputs. Any assistant that speaks the protocol can then discover those tools and call them. Why a standard helps Before a shared protocol, every pairing of assistant and service needed its own integration. A standard turns that many-to-many problem into one-to-many: a service writes one server, and every compatible assistant can use it. For a small team, that means an assistant can read the task tracker, look at a workflow's last run or draft an email without anyone writing glue code. What a tool description really is The interesting part isn't the transport. It's that an MCP tool is a described action: a name, what it does, which inputs it takes and what comes back. That is the same discipline good business processes need anyway. An organisation that can describe its own operations that clearly is most of the way to being usable by agents, whether through MCP or through its website. Where it fits, and where it doesn't Connectors are excellent for exploring, for one-off tasks and for an operator working alongside an assistant. They are a weaker fit for the steps that must run the same way every time. An assistant deciding, on each run, how to call a tool brings variation and cost to work that should be boring. The approach used here treats a connector as a fallback. Routine work goes through scripts that call each provider's API in the same way every time, kept in a repository and tested. When no script covers a need yet, the connector is used, the use is noted, and writing the script that replaces it becomes the next piece of work. The practical takeaway - Use MCP connectors to look around and to handle the unusual. - Turn anything you do through a connector twice into a script. - Describe your own operations as if they were tools. It helps people, and it's what agents will need.

posts.title: n8n or Windmill? Decide who owns the process first
posts.excerpt: Workflow tools overlap, so the useful question isn't which one is better. It's which tool owns the order of the steps, and which one only talks to vendors. Keeping those apart is what lets you swap a vendor without touching the process.
posts.text: n8n and Windmill can both run a multi-step workflow, call an API and wait for a person. Comparing them feature by feature goes nowhere, because each can do most of what the other does. The question that settles it is different: which tool owns the process, and which one only integrates? Two jobs that look like one A business process has two kinds of work in it: - The process itself. The order of the steps, who approves what, what happens when a step fails, and the record of what happened. This is the part the business cares about and should be able to read. - Talking to vendors. Calling a mail provider, a spreadsheet, a payment service. Credentials, retries, each vendor's quirks. When both live in the same canvas, the vendor details leak into the process. Changing email providers then means editing the business workflow, and nobody can say for sure what else moved. The split used here In this setup, Windmill owns the process. Its flows are files in a repository, with typed inputs, explicit steps and a clear stop when anything fails. Windmill never calls a vendor directly. n8n integrates. Each n8n workflow answers one named capability, such as "send a broadcast for this post", for one customer's vendor. It holds the vendor credentials, does the vendor-specific retries, and replies in one shape: succeeded, failed, or unknown. Between them sits a short list of operations named by what they do, never by who does it. The process asks for "send the broadcast", and a per-customer binding decides that, today, Brevo answers. What it buys - Swapping a vendor touches one workflow and one binding. The process doesn't change. - The process stays readable. A flow is a handful of steps, not a wall of HTTP nodes. - Failures are honest. A vendor problem comes back as "failed" or "unknown", and the process stops for a person rather than retrying something that may already have happened. When not to bother For a one-off automation with a single vendor, this is overhead: build it in whichever tool you know. The split pays off the second time the same process runs for a different customer, or the first time a vendor changes.

posts.title: Wiring the newsletter with Brevo: adopt before you build
posts.excerpt: Subscriber lists, consent and unsubscribe are solved problems with legal weight. This blog hands all three to Brevo and keeps its own code to the part that's actually specific: one email per published post.
posts.text: The quickest way to get a newsletter wrong is to build one. A list of email addresses looks like a small table, but behind it sit consent records, double opt-in, unsubscribe links in every email, bounce handling and the rules that come with each. A mail provider does all of that already, and is accountable for it. So the rule for this blog's newsletter was simple: adopt before you build. Brevo owns the list, the confirmation email, consent and unsubscribe. The site never stores an address. Subscribing: a plain form The subscribe box on every page is Brevo's own form, posted as ordinary HTML. It works with scripts turned off. Brevo sends a confirmation email first, and nothing else arrives until the reader clicks it. If the form can't be configured for some reason, the page falls back to an email link rather than showing a broken box. Sending: one email per post The part that is specific to this blog is when to send: once, when a post is published. That has one hard rule — the same post must never go out twice, even if a deploy runs again or something retries. The design keeps that rule in the place that can see it. Each campaign is named after the post it announces. Before sending, the workflow looks for a campaign with that name. If one exists and was sent, it stops. If one exists as a draft, because an earlier send failed halfway, it sends that draft instead of creating another. The provider's own record becomes the sent-log, so there is no second database to keep in step. Off until it's proven Broadcasting stays switched off until it has been tested end to end against a test list: a test subscriber who confirms, and a test post that produces exactly one campaign. Until then, subscribers simply accumulate in Brevo and nobody receives anything unexpected. The general lesson Look at each piece of a feature and ask who should be accountable for it. Consent and delivery belong to the provider. The decision of what to send, and when, belongs to you. Building only the second part is less code and far less risk.

posts.title: Why this blog is a static Astro site
posts.excerpt: A newsletter-first blog needs fast pages, typed content and nothing on a server to patch. Astro gives that without giving up components, and it compares well with Hugo for a site that will grow an assistant.
posts.text: Every publication starts with the same temptation: pick a platform with everything built in. For a site whose job is to publish writing and collect subscribers, "everything" mostly means things to maintain. This blog is a static site built with Astro, and the reasons are worth writing down, because they apply to most small organisations. What the site actually has to do The list is short: - Render articles and a home page quickly, on any phone. - Keep each post's metadata consistent: title, excerpt, date, issue number, tags. - Collect email subscribers without running a database. - Leave room to add an on-page assistant later without rewriting the site. None of that needs a server. A folder of HTML files on ordinary hosting does all of it, and there's nothing to patch at night. Typed content, not loose files Astro's content collections let a post's frontmatter be checked against a schema at build time. If a post is missing its excerpt, or its date isn't a date, the build fails before anything reaches readers. That sounds minor until the same data feeds more than one page: the home list, the article header, and, later, a machine-readable index that an assistant reads. Components when you need them Astro pages are HTML first, with components for the parts that repeat: the subscribe box, the header, the connected-node motif. Scripts are opt-in, so a page ships no JavaScript unless it needs some. Compared with Hugo Hugo is also a fine static generator, and faster at building very large sites. The difference here is mostly ergonomics. Astro's components, its typed collections and its plain JavaScript ecosystem are closer to how the rest of this stack is built, so adding a small module later, such as an assistant, doesn't mean learning a second templating language. For a site of a few dozen pages, build speed isn't the constraint. The trade-off A static site can't do anything on its own after it's built. Forms post to a service that owns the data, and anything dynamic runs in the visitor's browser. For a blog that's the right trade: fewer moving parts, and the services that hold people's data are the ones built to hold it.
